title: Chi-Square Test
body:
Blocks 3 and 4 test means and proportions, which need numbers. **$\chi^2$ is what you use when the
data is categorical and all you have are counts.** One statistic covers both jobs:

$$
\chi^2 = \sum_{\text{cells}} \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}
$$

observed minus expected, squared so signs cannot cancel, divided by expected so a discrepancy of 5
counts for more in a cell expecting 10 than in one expecting 1000. Large $\chi^2$ means the counts
do not look like what the null predicted, so it is always a right-tailed test.

## Goodness of fit

One categorical variable against a claimed distribution. $H_0$ says the proportions are as
specified; $E_i = np_i$ under that claim.

```
A die is rolled 120 times. H0: fair, so E = 20 for every face.

face      1   2   3   4   5   6
observed 16  22  25  18  14  25
(O-E)²/E 0.8 0.2 1.25 0.2 1.8 1.25   ->  chi-sq = 5.5
df = 6 - 1 = 5,  critical value at 0.05 is 11.07
5.5 < 11.07, so fail to reject: no evidence the die is unfair
```

Degrees of freedom are $k - 1$: once five face counts are known the sixth is forced by the total.
Same accounting as everywhere else in the course, see [[Variance]].

This is also a real tool outside coursework. Testing whether a generator's output matches uniform
is a goodness-of-fit test, which is one of the standard checks on [[Random Numbers]], and ranking
candidate decryptions by how closely their letter frequencies match English is the same test used
as a scoring function in classical cryptanalysis. See [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]].

## Contingency tables

Two categorical variables, cross-tabulated. $H_0$ is that they are **independent**, which makes this
[[Conditional Probability]]'s definition turned into a test: under independence
$P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$, so the expected count in a cell is

$$
E_{ij} = \frac{(\text{row } i \text{ total})(\text{column } j \text{ total})}{n}
$$

with $\text{df} = (r-1)(c-1)$, again the number of cells you could fill freely before the margins
force the rest.

**The $2 \times 2$ case is the [[Confusion Matrix]].** Four counts, two binary variables, and the
$\chi^2$ test asks whether the predictions carry any information about the truth. A classifier no
better than chance produces a table $\chi^2$ cannot distinguish from independent. That equivalence
is the reason [[Type I and Type II Errors]] and this note describe the same grid, and it is the
cleanest bridge in the vault between [[STATISTICS]] and the fourth-year computer science evaluation set.

## Conditions and cautions

- **Expected counts should be at least 5 in every cell.** The $\chi^2$ distribution is a continuous
  approximation to a discrete count problem and it breaks down on sparse tables. Merge categories,
  or use Fisher's exact test.
- Use the **counts**, never the percentages. Feeding proportions in destroys the sample size the
  test depends on, and a difference significant on $n = 1000$ is not on $n = 10$.
- The test says the variables are related. It says nothing about **how**, nothing about direction,
  and nothing about causation. Look at which cells contributed most of the sum for that.
